area: Area VII. Slow Flight and Stalls
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain why a wing stalls, spot the cues of a power-off stall, and fly a power-off stall from the approach or landing configuration and recover the AFH way: lower the nose first, level the wings, then add power and climb away.
why: Many stall/spin accidents happen in power-off situations near the ground, such as the turn from base to final or a low, sinking final [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104a]]. Knowing the cues and the recovery cold is what keeps a small mistake in the pattern from becoming a crash.

warmup: On final, the airplane is sinking low and you pull the nose up to stretch the glide without adding power. What happens to your angle of attack, and where does that end?

key_terms.def: Angle between the wing's chord line and the relative wind.
The AOA where airflow separates and the wing stalls. About 16 to 20 degrees, depending on design. Same AOA every time for a given airplane in a given configuration.
Loss of lift when the critical AOA is exceeded. Can happen at any airspeed, attitude or power setting.
AOA has caused a stall warning but has not yet reached the critical AOA.
Critical AOA exceeded. Usually a nose-down pitch you can't readily stop, maybe with a roll.
Lift divided by the airplane's weight, in G. Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor.
Stall speed or minimum steady flight speed in the landing configuration.
Stall speed or minimum steady flight speed in a specified configuration.
A second stall caused by rushing the recovery before enough flying speed returns.
A stall above 1 G, so at a higher-than-normal indicated airspeed (turns, pull-ups).
A stall with aileron one way and rudder the other, e.g. a skidding base-to-final turn.
An aggravated stall with yaw that leads to autorotation and a corkscrew path down.

chunks.title: Angle of attack: why a wing stalls

body.p: AOA is the angle at which the wing's chord meets the relative wind. As AOA increases, lift and drag increase. Past the critical AOA, air separates from the top of the wing, lift drops and drag rises. That is a stall [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].
The stall comes from too much AOA, not too little airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. A wing can be stalled at any airspeed, attitude and power setting [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

bullets: A given airplane always stalls at the same AOA, no matter the airspeed, weight, load factor or density altitude [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
Critical AOA is about 16 to 20 degrees, depending on design [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
At low speed you need a high AOA to hold altitude. Slow down enough and the needed AOA reaches the critical AOA [[1:100|PHAK 5-3]].
The wing doesn't stop making lift in a stall. It just can't make enough to hold level flight [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

body.p: Why the nose drops: the center of lift sits behind the CG. At the stall the tail force weakens, the nose pitches down, AOA decreases and the wing flies again. Much altitude can be lost in this cycle [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]].

callout.text: Stall = AOA problem. Fix = lower AOA. The elevator controls AOA.

check.q: Can you stall at cruise airspeed?
check.a: Yes. A stall happens whenever the critical AOA is exceeded, at any airspeed, attitude or power setting [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

body.p: The published 1G stall speed is only good in unaccelerated, coordinated flight at one weight (usually max gross) and one CG (usually most forward) [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Change any of these and the stall speed changes.

head: Factor
Effect
rows: Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor. A 45-knot stall speed becomes 90 knots at 4 G [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100g]]. A level 60-degree bank is 2 G and stalls 41 percent above the 1G stall speed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].
More weight means higher stall speed, since the wing needs more AOA for more lift [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100i]].
Stalling AOA is often reached at a higher airspeed; more back pressure needed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100h]].

Easier to stall by accident with light back pressure; a spin may go flat, and flat spin recovery is often impossible [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100h]] [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100h]]. Beyond the aft limit you may not be able to lower the nose to recover [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].
Flaps generally lower stall speed. The white arc starts at the landing-configuration stall speed, below the start of the green arc (clean) [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100c]] [[13:8|AC 61-67C 100c]].
Nose-high with power, part of the thrust helps hold the airplane up [[1:100|PHAK 5-3]]. Power-off, you lose that help and the stall cues are weaker [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].
Little or no effect on indicated stall speed. Fly the POH indicated speeds at any elevation [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]].
Even a small amount raises stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100k]]. As little as 0.8 mm of ice on the upper wing cuts lift by 25 percent [[1:123|PHAK 5-26]].

body.p: **Attitude:** you can stall in any attitude, so the view out the window alone is not a sure stall cue [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. **Yaw:** at low speed, torque, slipstream and P-factor yaw the airplane left, so you need more right rudder the closer you get to the stall [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Yaw at the stall is what turns a stall into a spin [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

check.q: Your airplane stalls at 50 knots straight and level. About what is the stall speed in a level 60-degree bank?
check.a: Load factor is 2 G, so about 41 percent higher: roughly 70 knots [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

chunks.title: Stall cues and the limits of stall warnings

body.p: **Airplane design.** Most trainers stall at the wing root first and outward to the tips. Some wings have washout (twist) so the tips fly at a lower AOA. Ailerons may still work in the stall, but using them before you lower AOA can deepen the stall at the tip and roll you further [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

**Power-off stall cues are softer.** Buffet and shaking are less noticeable than in a power-on stall. The main cue may be the elevator full aft against the stops and a high descent rate [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

head: Sense
What you notice
rows: Controls get mushy, need bigger movements, and react slower [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]
The sound of air along the airplane changes as speed drops [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]
Not foolproof, since you can stall in any attitude; still keep pitch awareness [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]
Nose-down pitch you can't readily stop, maybe with a roll [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]

body.p: **Stall warning devices (range and limits):**

bullets: Certification requires a clear and distinctive stall warning with enough margin to prevent an inadvertent stall [[35:33|14 CFR 23.2150(a)]]. It may come from natural buffet or from a device [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Many stall warning devices alert the pilot 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].
Most vintage, and many light-sport and experimental, airplanes have no stall warning device [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
A stall warning system can fail. Then use buffet, loss of roll authority, or inability to stop a descent [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
With ice, the stall may come with little or none of the usual cues [[13:10|AC 61-67C 102a]]. Don't rely on stall warning devices with ice on the airplane [[24:259|AFH 13-10]].

AOA indicators show your margin to the critical AOA, but are limited by calibration, unheated probes or vanes, indicator type, flap setting and wing contamination [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:119|AFH 5-14]]. Some account for flaps, some don't [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

check.q: In a power-off stall with no stall horn, what may be the strongest cue?
check.a: The elevator full aft against the stops and a high descent rate [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

chunks.title: How power-off stalls happen (and how to prevent them)

body.p: Power-off stalls are also called approach-to-landing stalls. Many stall/spin accidents happen in these situations [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104a]]:

bullets: Crossed-control turns from base to final (skidding or slipping turn).
Trying to fix a high sink rate on final with only more nose-up pitch.
Poor airspeed control on final or elsewhere in the pattern.
Trying to stretch a glide after an engine failure, or being low on the approach [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

body.p: **The base-to-final trap.** A tailwind on base makes you turn late and overshoot. The pilot steepens the bank, pulls back, and adds inside rudder to swing the nose around. Bank increases, the nose drops, the pilot pulls more, and a stall here can quickly become a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

callout.text: Overshooting final? Go around. In the pattern, be reluctant to bank more than 30 degrees and never skid the turn to fix an overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: **Stall warnings during normal operations.** In slow flight, any more AOA, more load factor or less power gives a stall warning. React to and correct any stall indication [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. A horn on climb-out or in the pattern is a warning, not background noise. One AFH case: a pilot departs a high, hot airport, keeps pitching up over rising terrain, the airplane stops climbing and the stall horn sounds [[24:101|AFH 4-15]].

**Spin awareness.** A spin needs a stall plus yaw. Yaw comes from wrong rudder, adverse yaw from aileron, engine/prop effects, or wind shear [[24:127|AFH 5-22]]. Keep the ball centered and don't let the nose yaw before you recover [[24:127|AFH 5-22]].

callout.text: Prevention: fly the POH approach speed, keep the ball centered, bank 30 degrees or less in the pattern, add power (not just pitch) when low, and go around early.

check.q: You overshoot the turn to final. What is the safest action?
check.a: Go around. Don't steepen past about 30 degrees or skid the turn [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: The most important action for an impending or full stall is to **reduce the AOA**. Pilots who went for power or held altitude first have lost control [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. Use the same recovery for impending and full stalls [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

head: AFH recovery template
Action
rows: Push until the stall warning stops [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Roll wings level; use rudder to stop yaw [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]
Smooth and coordinated; avoid a secondary stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]

body.p: In a single-engine trainer with no autopilot, you use four steps: lower AOA, level wings, power, return to the flightpath [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

bullets: Power reduces altitude loss but does not end a stall. Only lowering AOA does [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
Too much forward pressure can hinder recovery by putting a negative load on the wing [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].
Don't level the wings before lowering AOA; aileron on a stalled wing can make it worse [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].
Never let the airspeed or tach reach the red line during a practice stall [[13:11|AC 61-67C 105]].

callout.text: PUSH - ROLL - POWER - CLIMB: nose down till the warning stops, wings level, power, back to the flightpath.

check.q: Why is "add full power" not the first step?
check.a: Power reduces altitude loss but does not eliminate a stall; only reducing AOA does [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

body.p: Generic AFH procedure. Speeds, flap settings and power come from your POH.

bullets: 1. **Clear the area** with clearing turns, looking at and below your altitude [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
2. **Pick an altitude** that lets you recover no lower than 1,500 ft AGL, or higher if the POH says so [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].
3. **Configure:** gear down (if retractable), carb heat on (if applicable), power back. Hold altitude until you slow to normal approach speed [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

4. **Stabilized descent:** lower the nose to the approach attitude to hold that speed. Extend flaps (landing configuration, or as the examiner asks) and adjust pitch to hold airspeed. Then power to idle [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]. Don't carry extra speed into the entry; it gives an abnormally nose-high attitude [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

5. **Induce the stall:** once stable, smoothly raise the nose to an attitude that will stall. Keep heading and wings level with coordinated aileron and rudder. Hold that attitude with elevator until the stall [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].
6. **Call the cues** (horn, buffet, mushy controls) and hold the attitude until the full stall: a nose-down pitch you can't readily stop [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
7. **Recover:** lower the nose until the stall warning stops, level the wings, stay coordinated, then add power. Right rudder may be needed as power comes in and the nose lowers [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

8. **Go around:** establish a positive rate of climb, then retract flaps and gear as needed [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]. Raise flaps in small steps [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]; flaps before gear unless the POH says otherwise [[24:183|AFH 9-12]]. Accelerate to VX or VY per the POH.
9. **Return** to the altitude, heading and airspeed the examiner gives you.

body.p: **Turning version:** use a shallow, constant, coordinated bank to simulate the base-to-final turn. The stall should normally come within about 90 degrees of heading change. A slip can stall the outer wing first; a skid can steepen the bank [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

head: ACS standard
Tolerance
rows: Completed no lower than 1,500 ft AGL (ACS PA.VII.B.S2)
Approach or landing configuration as the evaluator specifies; coordinated throughout (ACS PA.VII.B.S3)
Acknowledge impending-stall cues, then recover promptly after the full stall (ACS PA.VII.B.S7)
Per the POH/AFM (ACS PA.VII.B.S8); configure per manufacturer and accelerate to VX or VY (ACS PA.VII.B.S9)
Altitude, heading and airspeed specified by the evaluator (ACS PA.VII.B.S10)

check.q: What three things do you do, in order, the moment the airplane fully stalls?
check.a: Lower the nose until the stall warning stops, level the wings with coordinated rudder, then add power [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

head: Stall
Cause
Fix
rows: Rushing the recovery: pulling the nose up abruptly before enough flying speed, or trying to break the stall with power only [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]]. Raising flaps too fast or holding a high climb attitude with flaps out can also cause one [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]].
Recover again: nose down until the warning stops, wings level, coordinate, power [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].
Stall above 1 G at a higher-than-normal speed, often in badly flown turns, pull-outs, or an overshot base-to-final turn [[24:124|AFH 5-19]]. More severe and often unexpected [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104c]].
Forward elevator to cut AOA, level wings, coordinate, power as needed [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Critical AOA exceeded with aileron one way and rudder the other. Little warning; can roll toward inverted and start a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Lower AOA until the warning stops, then roll level and coordinate before a spiral or spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

body.p: On the private checkride these are knowledge items. Secondary and cross-control stalls are demonstration-only (only CFI applicants may have to perform them), and accelerated stalls are for commercial and CFI applicants [[24:124|AFH 5-19]] [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

callout.text: In a cross-controlled stall, the spin usually goes toward the rudder you're holding, no matter which wingtip is up [[13:12|AC 61-67C 109]].

check.q: After a power-off stall you yank the nose up to stop the descent and the horn comes back. What happened and what do you do?
check.a: A secondary stall from rushing the recovery. Lower the nose until the warning stops, level the wings, coordinate, add power, then climb [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] [[24:124|AFH 5-19]].

head: Hazard
Effect on power-off stalls
What to do
rows: A vertical gust can suddenly raise AOA and stall the airplane at a much higher airspeed, often on a gusty approach [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].
Fly a higher than normal approach speed in moderate or severe turbulence or strong crosswinds [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].
Downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and headwind losses of 30-90 knots; on approach it can force you to the ground short of the runway [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].
Be alert near thunderstorms and fronts; watch for an intense rain shaft, virga or a ring of blowing dust [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].
Indicated stall speed hardly changes, but true airspeed is higher [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]]. Less power means pitching up to climb can bleed speed until the horn sounds [[24:101|AFH 4-15]].
Fly the POH indicated speeds; don't trade airspeed for climb [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100j]].

body.p: **Collision hazards.** Stall practice involves big changes in altitude and heading. Clear the area at and below your altitude first [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Clearing turns make sure the next maneuver won't go into another airplane's path [[24:33|AFH 1-12]]. High wings block the view above and low wings below; banking uncovers blind spots [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].

**Distractions.** Stalls from poor airspeed control happen most when the pilot is busy with something else: a checklist, an engine restart, a windy pattern, a chart, or reaching for something on the floor or back seat [[13:9|AC 61-67C 101]]. Fly first; do the secondary task only when the airplane is under control.

**SRM.** Single-pilot resource management means managing all resources available to you, including task management and situational awareness [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]]. In this task: brief the maneuver, use the before-landing checks to configure [[24:116|AFH 5-11]], keep scanning for traffic, and keep track of where you are and your altitude above the ground.

check.q: Why can a gust stall the airplane above the published stall speed?
check.a: A vertical gust suddenly changes the relative wind and raises the AOA, so the airplane can stall at a much higher airspeed [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].

body.p: From the AFH list for intentional stalls [[24:126|AFH 5-21]]:

bullets: Not clearing the area.
Pulling too fast during entry, causing an accelerated stall.
Not holding a constant bank in turning stalls.
Poor rudder coordination during the stall and recovery.
Recovering before the critical AOA when a full stall is asked for.
Not holding nose-down input until the stall warning stops.
Leveling the wings, or adding power, before lowering AOA.
Forgetting to roll wings level after the warning stops.
Secondary stall during recovery; too much forward pressure (low or negative G); too much airspeed buildup.
Losing situational awareness and not returning to the assigned flightpath.

callout.text: On the go-around, a sudden full flap retraction can cause a loss of lift and settling [[24:182|AFH 9-11]]. Climb first, then flaps in steps.

check.q: Name two errors that lead to a secondary stall.
check.a: Pulling the nose up too soon or too hard in recovery, and trying to recover with power alone or raising flaps too fast [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]].

scenario.title: Gusty day, tailwind on base
scenario.setup: You're solo in the pattern on a gusty afternoon. The wind gives you a tailwind on base. Tower asks you to report a traffic sighting just as you start the turn to final. You look for the traffic, turn late, and see you'll fly through the extended centerline. The airspeed is a few knots slow and the airplane is sinking low.

questions.q: What is tempting you to do, and why is it dangerous?
questions.a: Steepen the bank, pull back and push inside rudder to swing the nose around. That is a skidding cross-control turn; a stall in it can quickly become a spin [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].
Go around. In the pattern be reluctant to bank past 30 degrees and never skid to fix an overshoot [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

questions.q: You're low and slow on final. Why not just raise the nose?
questions.a: Fixing a high sink rate with only more pitch is a classic power-off stall/spin cause [[13:11|AC 61-67C 104a]]. Add power and keep the airspeed.

questions.q: How do the gusts change your plan?
questions.a: A gust can raise the AOA and stall you at a higher airspeed. Fly a higher than normal approach speed in moderate or severe turbulence or strong crosswinds [[13:9|AC 61-67C 100l]].

questions.q: The stall horn chirps in the turn. What do you do?
questions.a: Treat it as a real warning: lower the nose to reduce AOA until it stops, level the wings, coordinate, add power, and go around [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

questions.q: During the go-around you raise all the flaps at once and pitch up steeply. What can happen?
questions.a: Settling or a secondary stall. Climb first, then raise flaps in small steps [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200f]].

questions.q: How did the traffic call contribute?
questions.a: Distraction. Poor airspeed control stalls are most likely when the pilot is busy with another task [[13:9|AC 61-67C 101]]. Fly the airplane first.

skills.do: Clear the area before the maneuver.
skills.practice: Do two clearing turns before every stall and say what you see. Look at and below your altitude [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

skills.do: Pick an entry altitude so the recovery ends no lower than 1,500 ft AGL.
skills.practice: Before each stall, say the ground elevation and your planned entry and minimum altitudes out loud.

skills.do: Set the approach or landing configuration the examiner asks for and stay coordinated.
skills.practice: Fly the setup from your before-landing checklist; keep the ball centered the whole time [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

skills.do: Establish a stabilized descent at approach speed.
skills.practice: Slow at constant altitude to approach speed, pitch to the approach attitude, add flaps, power to idle, and wait until airspeed stops changing [[24:122|AFH 5-17]].

skills.do: Smoothly raise the nose to a stall-inducing attitude.
skills.practice: Raise the nose smoothly, not quickly; pulling too fast gives an accelerated stall [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].

skills.do: Hold heading ±10° straight, or a bank of 20° or less ±10° in turns, while inducing the stall.
skills.practice: Pick a point on the horizon (straight) or hold a constant shallow bank (turning); stall within about 90° of turn [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

skills.do: Call out impending-stall cues, then recover promptly after the full stall.
skills.practice: Say "horn, buffet" as they come; hold the attitude until the nose drops on its own, then recover at once [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
Chair-fly: push until the warning stops, roll level, power, climb [[24:121|AFH 5-16]]. Check your POH for any differences.

skills.do: Configure per the manufacturer and accelerate to VX or VY.
skills.practice: After positive climb, raise flaps in steps and gear as needed; know your POH's VX, VY and flap retraction speeds [[24:182|AFH 9-11]] [[24:183|AFH 9-12]].

skills.do: Return to the altitude, heading and airspeed the examiner gives.
skills.practice: Note entry heading and altitude before you start; climb back and level off on them.
Brief the maneuver, use checklists, keep scanning for traffic, and keep task priorities: aviate first [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]].

options: Airspeed falls below the white arc
The critical angle of attack is exceeded
The nose rises above the horizon
quiz.why: A stall is the result of exceeding the critical AOA, not insufficient airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

quiz.q: The critical AOA of a typical airplane is about:
quiz.why: Critical AOA varies from about 16 to 20 degrees depending on design [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]].

quiz.q: In a level, coordinated 60-degree bank, the airplane stalls at a speed about:
options: The same as the 1G stall speed
quiz.why: Load factor is 2 G and the stall speed is 41 percent higher than the 1G stall speed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

quiz.q: In a power-off 1G stall, the predominant cue may be:
options: Elevator full aft against the stops and a high descent rate
quiz.why: Power-off cues are less noticeable; the main cue may be full up elevator and a high descent rate [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

quiz.q: The first action in recovering from a stall in a trainer with no autopilot is:
quiz.why: Reducing AOA is the most important action; in a trainer it is the actual first step [[24:120|AFH 5-15]] [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

quiz.q: Many stall warning devices alert the pilot about how far before the stall?
quiz.why: Many stall warning devices alert the pilot 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C 103]].

quiz.q: A secondary stall is most often caused by:
options: Rushing the recovery before regaining enough flying speed
quiz.why: A secondary stall comes from trying to hasten the recovery before the airplane has regained sufficient flying speed [[13:11|AC 61-67C 106]].

quiz.q: You overshoot final in a turn from base. The safest action is to:
options: Add inside rudder to bring the nose around
Raise the nose and slow down
quiz.why: The safest action for an overshoot is a go-around; don't skid the turn or bank past about 30 degrees [[24:125|AFH 5-20]].

takeaways: A stall is too much AOA, at any airspeed, attitude or power setting.
Load factor, weight, CG, flaps and ice change the stall speed; altitude hardly changes indicated stall speed.
Power-off cues are subtle: full aft elevator and a high sink rate. Stall horns can fail or be absent.
Recovery: nose down until the warning stops, wings level, power, climb. AOA first, always.
Overshot final? Go around. No skidding turns, 30 degrees bank or less in the pattern.
Finish no lower than 1,500 ft AGL; heading ±10°, or bank 20° or less ±10°.
cfi_notes: Teach the same recovery for impending and full stalls [[24:122|AFH 5-17]]. Students often stop pushing as soon as the nose is level; insist the push continues until the warning stops.

Per AC 61-67C, have the student fly a full-flap power-off stall and note the altitude loss, then repeat with a distraction and show how flap retraction errors cause a secondary stall [[13:17|AC 61-67C 200e]].
Common checkride issue: the applicant recovers at the first horn when the examiner wants a full stall. ACS S7 wants cues acknowledged, then recovery after the full stall.
Watch for pulling too fast on entry (accelerated stall) and for carrying extra airspeed into the entry, which gives a very nose-high attitude [[24:122|AFH 5-17]] [[24:126|AFH 5-21]].
AFH (41 percent) and AC 61-67C (40 percent) round the 60-degree-bank stall speed increase differently [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] [[13:7|AC 61-67C 100b]]; either is fine.
Ask: "Why not add power first?" and "What does the ball do in a skidding turn?" These test real understanding, not memorized steps.
gaps: Airplane-specific speeds (approach speed, VSO, VS1, VX, VY), flap settings, flap retraction speeds and the manufacturer's stall recovery procedure (ACS S8, S9) come from the POH/AFM.
The sources don't discuss when a stall warning normally sounds near touchdown in a landing flare; covered here only generally (react to any stall warning in flight).
Turning power-off stalls: the AFH gives no bank angle number (just "shallow"); the 20 degree limit comes only from the ACS.
